name: Two souls and transmigration
plain_explanation: Human beings have two souls -- an immortal one made by God, located in the head, and a mortal one made by lesser gods, located in the chest, which is the source of pleasure, pain, fear, anger, and hope; after death, cowardly or wicked men are reborn as women, and the foolish or unphilosophical are reborn as birds, land animals, or, for the very stupidest, fishes.
precise_definition: Timaeus's psychology dividing the human soul into an immortal, divinely created part housed in the head and a mortal part, created by the lesser gods and subject to the passions, housed in the breast, combined with a doctrine of transmigration in which moral and intellectual failure in one life determines a lower form of embodiment in the next.
why_it_mattered: It exemplifies the parts of the dialogue Russell regards as closer to imaginative 'play of fancy' than to Plato's serious philosophical commitments.
historical_origin: Continuous with the transmigration doctrine already set out in the Phaedo (previous chapter), itself of Orphic-Pythagorean origin.
examples: 'Innocent light-minded men, who think that astronomy can be learnt by looking at the stars without knowledge of mathematics, will become birds.'
connection_to_politics_or_religion: Continuous with Orphic-Pythagorean doctrines of transmigration.
